note: Which committer identity owns which paths (plan.md 6.2.1). git records no session, so a seat declares itself: the committer is the seat and the author stays the person. Read by check 41.
adopt: Put the seat in the worktree's own git config and git uses it: `git config extensions.worktreeConfig true` once, then `git config --worktree committer.name 'seat:<name>'` and `--worktree committer.email <name>@seat.invalid`. Git has read committer.name and committer.email since v2.22, so no environment prefix is needed -- verified on 2.50.1: the commit's committer is the seat and the author stays the person. An env prefix (GIT_COMMITTER_NAME=... GIT_COMMITTER_EMAIL=... git commit) still works and is what a shared working copy with no worktree config has to use. This note said until 2026-09-18 that git does not read those keys and that a context reset therefore downgrades the next commit to the person's identity; both were wrong, and the config survives a reset on its own (6.2.3).
addresses: seat.invalid is reserved by RFC 2606 and can never route. A seat identity is a label, not a mailbox.
boundaries: owns holds boundary names as check 41 derives them from the path, using the same table check 35 counts: design, microscope_agent, simulation_agent, librarian_agent, bridge. An agent's CLAUDE.md and .claude/ are the design seat's, and so is all of contracts/.
unknown_committer_note: report: a committer absent from this list is reported rather than refused, so a seat that has not adopted an identity is not blocked. refuse: fail-closed. The precondition for switching is that every seat has adopted one, the person included -- a person committing by hand would otherwise be refused on the first day, and that bypass is what becomes the habit. Note also what report costs: an unattributed commit gets no checking at all, because nothing says whose paths those were.
structure: Nine seats as of 2026-09-17: architecture (1), manager (4), execution (4). Manager and execution pair up per agent. The tiers hold no extra permission -- architecture and the managers are all Tier 0 and touch no instrument; what the tier gives is an order, not power (6.2).
one_identity_per_session: A seat is a session, not a role. Two sessions sharing one identity is not a seat, it is a hole: check 41 cannot tell them apart and passes their mixture. This happened twice on 2026-09-17 -- two sessions at the root both being the design seat by definition, then four sessions sharing manager@seat.invalid. Both times the check passed and the pass was the defect.
growth: Execution seats may grow past one per agent (decided 2026-09-17). When a second session for one agent opens, give it its own identity -- librarian-2@seat.invalid, simulation-2@seat.invalid, microscope-3@seat.invalid -- with the same `owns` and no `paths`, rather than letting it share microscope@seat.invalid. Paths that cannot honestly be divided stay undivided: a narrowing invented to look tidy refuses correct work, and a seat that gets refused for correct work reaches for --no-verify. What a shared identity costs is attribution, which is the one thing this file exists to give; what a shared path costs is refusal, which the worktree merge covers instead (6.2.1). Adding a seat is an edit to this file alone -- check 41 reads `owns`, `paths` and `excludes` as data and needs no change -- and this file is the architecture seat's, so growing the team crosses exactly one boundary. Used for real on 2026-09-18 with librarian-2, and two consequences showed up that the rule did not name. An unregistered committer's ordinary commit is PENDING under unknown_committer: report -- but --strict counts PENDING as failure, so the mode CI is told to run goes red on every commit from an unregistered seat. And a merge by an unregistered committer is FAIL regardless of that setting, because check 35 does not read merges and the merge's own contribution would be checked by nothing. So registering a new seat is not bookkeeping to be done later: it is what keeps the gate usable from that seat's first commit. The example in this note used to say microscope-2, and that name was then spent on an A/B variant and deferred -- so on 2026-09-19 the next microscope session arrived at exactly the question the example was supposed to answer. An example naming a specific identity goes stale when that identity is used; the rule is the shape, not the name.
enforced_from_note: The commit that turned the session boundary from a convention into a gate. Checks 35 and 41 report rather than fail for anything at or before it. Two independent reasons, both checked on 2026-09-17: before f971c40 the boundary was written in 6.2 but nothing refused a crossing, and every commit in that stretch is the person's own -- who owns every boundary anyway (see the human seat). Exactly three commits are affected (0ea116e, e6a87f1, 72d17fc), all of them contracts/ and librarian_agent/ together while one design seat held both and kb/ was a hand-curated store.
why_an_epoch_and_not_a_proxy: Using the presence of seats.json in the parent was proposed and is narrower than it looks: that file is check 41's mechanism, and check 35 counts boundaries without reading it, so the proxy would explain one check by the other's history. An epoch says the thing directly and can be moved with a reason attached. It is deliberately not fixed by registering kyuchoi@stanford.edu as a seat -- the human entry's own note refuses that, because a git default listed here would be inherited by every session and check 41 would stop meaning anything.
what_an_epoch_costs: It hides real crossings made before it. That is acceptable only because the period is fully accounted for -- three commits, all the person's, all inspected. Moving this forward again would not be: it would be pointing the gate away from work it should have caught. If history before an epoch ever needs auditing, audit it by hand rather than by moving the line.

seats.registered_late: Eight commits went out under this identity before this entry existed, from bfa02e7 to 597ab96 on 2026-09-19. Architecture owns this file and that session was unreachable for the whole stretch, so the seat committed rather than stopping, and every one of the eight says in its own message that the identity was unlisted and why. Under `unknown_committer: report` those were PENDING at check 41 and red under --strict, AND THEY STAY THAT WAY. This field claimed registration was retroactive when it was written, and that is wrong: check 41 resolves a committer against the registry as it stood at the COMMIT'S PARENT, for the reason its own docstring gives -- judging old commits against today's boundaries turns history red whenever a path moves between seats, and a sweep that reddens on normal activity is one nobody runs. A registration takes effect from the next commit on. Off a run: twelve commits under this seat, the eight before 4541151 permanently PENDING and the four after it attributed. The rule the next seat needs is REGISTER FIRST, COMMIT SECOND -- which is what the `growth` note means by registration keeping the gate usable from a seat's first commit, and what this entry is the counter-example to.
seats.written_by_the_seat_it_registers: IRREGULAR, AND FLAGGED RATHER THAN QUIET. This entry was written by librarian-3 itself, on the person's direct instruction of 2026-09-20, because the architecture session was gone and the person owns every boundary. It is still the shape this file is architecture's in order to prevent -- the architecture entry's own note says the tier being constrained must not own the file that says what it may touch, and an execution seat writing its own registry row is that with the subject changed. What makes it tolerable is narrowness and daylight: the row grants nothing this seat did not already have, `owns` is the same as librarian and librarian-2, no `paths` were invented, and this field exists so architecture reviews it rather than inherits it. Rewrite or reword it freely; the thing to check is that `owns` was not widened. REVIEWED 2026-09-20 AND THE REVIEW MISSED SOMETHING. Architecture checked that `owns` was not widened, found it was not, and accepted the entry -- while `registered_late` carried a false claim that registration is retroactive. The field says what to check and architecture checked only that, which is not a review of the document. The seat that wrote the entry found the error afterwards and raised it. A review scoped to one question answers one question.

seats.shared_in_contracts: Everything else under contracts/ is held by all four managers and is not divided: validate.py, schemas/common.schema.json, units.json, observables.json, validation_limits.json, hooks/, examples/ and the card schemas both executing agents use. There check 41 gives attribution and not refusal -- `paths` starting at contracts/ looks like a division and is not one, and this line is here so the registry does not imply a boundary it cannot hold. What guards that surface is the worktree merge (6.2.1), not this file.
seats.why_not_more: Moving validate.py and the shared schemas up to the architecture seat was proposed on 2026-09-17 and refused. The argument for it was sound -- a seat that can edit the code that checks it is the same shape excludes was written against -- but it does not survive being followed through. Architecture would then implement checks, against 6.2's 'specify, do not implement' and against the check-42 order that has the manager implement and architecture declare; and architecture writing the gate is still a seat checked by code it wrote, one tier up. The regress does not end inside the repository. It ends at an enforcement point no seat controls: a required status check on the remote. That is unavailable here -- branch protection needs a paid plan on a private repository -- so the honest state is that the shared core is guarded by review at merge, and this note says so.

seats.excludes_note: Enforced by check 41 since 607c3e9, which the manager seat wrote against its own boundary. It subtracts from what owns and paths grant, and is tested before the narrowing so the refusal names the real reason. Verified in a throwaway clone in both directions: manager is refused on contracts/seats.json and allowed elsewhere under contracts/, architecture is the reverse. This note said DECLARED, NOT ENFORCED while that was true; a registry that understates its protection is the same error as one that overstates it, so it is corrected here rather than left to age.
seats.why_divided: On 2026-09-17 four sessions each reported being the manager seat and the person confirmed that all four are. Sharing one identity made check 41 decorative for the whole tier: three commits stand under manager@seat.invalid and git cannot say which session made any of them. 6.2.1 prescribes dividing paths before opening a second seat at one position; this is that division, four ways.
seats.what_is_not_divided: contracts/ itself. Each manager needs the schemas, the vocabulary, the units registry and the validator, and no path split expresses that. Giving the core to one seat was proposed and refused: it serialises every schema and validator change through one session, which is the opposite of what the tier was built for. So all four hold contracts/, and there check 41 gives attribution rather than refusal -- the commit still says which session, but no crossing can be refused. On each agent's CLAUDE.md and .claude/ the division is real and the check refuses.
seats.what_protects_the_core: Nothing, at refusal level, since worktrees were reverted on 2026-09-18. This line said the worktree merge guarded it: two managers editing validate.py in separate worktrees would collide visibly at merge. With one working copy they overwrite each other silently again, which happened twice on 2026-09-17. What remains is attribution -- the commit says which session -- plus the convention not to use git add -A and the commit gate. The merge-awareness in checks 35 and 41 stays correct and currently guards nothing.

seats.note: The pre-D12 identity, kept valid through the migration. It is the undivided seat that architecture and manager replace: two sessions at the root were both the design seat by definition, and while they shared this identity check 41 passed their mixture -- which is what c13e742 was. 6.2.1 prescribed dividing `paths` before opening a second one; D12 is that division. Retire this entry once every top-tier session has adopted its own identity, and not before -- an identity removed while a session still uses it turns every commit from that session into an unknown committer.

The person writes approvals/ and envelope/safety.json, which no seat may (2.1 rule 7, 6.1), so this seat owns every boundary. It is deliberately an opt-in identity rather than the git default: if the default were listed here, every session would pass check 41 by inheriting it and the check would mean nothing.

paths_field: Optional, per seat: a list of path prefixes narrowing the seat inside the boundaries it owns. It exists for the case 6.2.1 names -- two seats that have to share a boundary must divide it first. A seat without it owns its boundaries whole.
dividing_a_boundary: When a boundary is split, the parts must still cover the whole. On 2026-09-18 they did not: .mcp.json sits in the design boundary and is declared in section 7, and after contracts/ and the agent instruction files were divided among architecture and four managers, no live seat's paths reached it -- only the retiring `design` identity and `human` could write it. A file nobody owns is not protected, it is stranded, and this one strands M1, M2 and M4: without the MCP registration no session can call the librarian, so the librarian-on completion condition cannot be met. The growth note says adding a seat touches this file alone; this is its mirror image, and the missing habit is to check the complement after every division. That is checkable -- every path section 7 declares inside a boundary should be reachable by some live seat -- and no check does it yet. Same shape again on 2026-09-20 with plan_ko.md: the design document of record is being renamed and the English rendering will take the old name, so for a while BOTH names are live and each has to be granted. Granted before the rename rather than with it, because check 41 resolves a committer against the registry at the commit's parent -- a rename commit cannot grant itself the name it creates.
a_vacated_identity_is_not_inherited: When a session closes, the next session for that agent gets a NEW identity rather than the freed one (decided 2026-09-19 for bridge-2). The one precedent for inheriting -- microscope-1 keeping its seat -- rested on inheriting the worktree and branch with it, and worktrees were reverted on 2026-09-18, so that precedent does not reach. The nearer precedent is microscope-3, which took a new name rather than the vacant microscope-2. What reuse costs is the thing this file exists to give: two sessions' commits collapse into one seat in the history with no way to tell them apart. The cost of not reusing is one line. And the vacated entry stays -- deleting `bridge` because it is idle would retroactively make the commits under it unknown-committer, which is what P16 and the microscope-2 note are about.
a_seat_is_minted_only_on_a_statement: A new seat is opened only when the person says a session was replaced, or when the occupying session says it has closed. Nothing else is evidence. On 2026-09-19 the architecture seat opened three seats that had to be withdrawn -- manager-bridge-2@seat.invalid, manager-librarian-2@seat.invalid, manager-simulation-2@seat.invalid -- on absence from a peer listing, on a failed message delivery, and on the person saying they had made a new session while the old one was still running and committing minutes earlier. All three signals were wrong, and the third is the trap: making a session is not the same event as a session ending. Splitting a live session's identity is one_identity_per_session broken from the other side -- one session's commits landing under two seats, which check 41 then reports as two seats' work. WIDENED 2026-09-20: the rule said replacement and a seat may also be opened CONCURRENTLY, which manager-librarian-2@seat.invalid is -- manager-librarian@seat.invalid is live and this is a second session beside it, the shape librarian-3@seat.invalid already has beside librarian@seat.invalid. The test is unchanged and it is the statement, not the reason: the person said it. What this instance adds is that the statement reached architecture by relay, from the seat requesting it, which 6.2.2 says is not a seating -- and it is not being treated as one. The person seated that session directly; this entry only records what they did, and is corrected if they say otherwise. The three names above are cited with their committer form so check 47 can see them; written bare, as they were until now, 47's two patterns do not match and the paragraph documenting notes_name_seats_and_nothing_checks_it reopened exactly that.
notes_name_seats_and_nothing_checks_it: A note here may name another seat, and until 2026-09-19 nothing verified that the name resolves. One did not: simulation-2's note pointed at simulation-1, which was never registered, while every commit from that agent went out under simulation@seat.invalid. Fourth time in one day that free text named something that had moved or never existed -- growth's example, a caller_id example, microscope-1's branch, this. Check 47 is assigned for it: every seat name appearing in this file's prose exists in `seats`. Cheap, and it had exactly one hit before the fix.
retired_names_note: Names cited in the prose above that are deliberately dead. simulation-1 was never registered and its branch is gone; simulation-2's note records that, and recording it means writing the name. Check 47 refuses any seat-shaped name in the prose that is neither registered nor listed here. A name goes here when a correction has to cite it, not when a seat is vacated -- a vacated seat keeps its entry and is simply unoccupied. manager-bridge-2 and manager-simulation-2 were opened on 2026-09-19 and withdrawn with zero commits; they are listed because the prose above cites them as the examples that earned the minting rule, and a cited dead name is what this field is for.
the_front_door_is_not_one_seats: README.md is on the four manager seats and on the undivided `manager` as well as on architecture, decided 2026-09-20. It is an UN-NARROWING and not a widening: README.md was always inside the `design` boundary every manager owns, it was never in anyone's `excludes`, and only `paths` kept them out -- so CLAUDE.md's rule that this file narrows and cannot widen is not touched. manager-librarian-2 established the distinction by running check 41's classifier rather than reading the registry, after telling the person the file was outside its boundary, which it was not. WHY IT HAD TO MOVE: contracts/hooks/pre-push, landed the same evening, made README.md refuse a push when it stops naming a top-level entry. That turned the front door into an artifact that can block every seat's push and could be written by one live seat. The first refusal proved it -- the fix was four names, and the only session able to type them was the architecture one. A gate whose only remedy sits in another seat gets bypassed with --no-verify rather than satisfied, which is the failure pre-commit's own comment was written against. It is the variant of `dividing_a_boundary`: there the parts stopped covering the whole and .mcp.json was an orphan nobody owned; here the parts cover it and one seat is a bottleneck. Both come of splitting a boundary without checking afterwards that the split still works. WHAT IT COSTS: the front door is now a shared surface like contracts/, so check 41 gives attribution and not refusal, and five seats can collide on it with nothing refusing -- which on 2026-09-20 was not hypothetical, that window opened at least six times in one evening across validate.py, plan.md, README.md and this file. Review at merge is what guards it, the same honest answer the managers' shared_in_contracts gives. AND THE OPEN QUESTION IS NARROWER THAN IT WAS: 11-11 asks whether every section 7 path reaches a live seat, and README did reach one. The question this raises is HOW MANY it reaches, which nothing checks and which only bites for paths a gate can refuse on.
